title: Crypto Gambling Records: What Canadians Should Keep
excerpt: Crypto casino play creates a paper trail most Canadians never think about. Here is what records to keep, why they matter, and how to stay organised.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Most Canadians who play at crypto casinos think about record-keeping exactly once: when something goes wrong. A withdrawal stalls, an account gets flagged for review, or an exchange asks where a deposit came from, and suddenly six months of transactions need reconstructing from memory. Keeping crypto gambling records is unglamorous, takes about two minutes a session, and is the difference between a five-minute support ticket and a genuine headache.

This guide covers what a Canadian player should record, why each item matters, and how to keep it without turning your hobby into bookkeeping.

Why crypto play needs records that fiat play does not

If you deposit at a casino with Interac, there is a clean, permanent trail sitting in your bank statement. Your bank knows who you are, the casino knows who you are, and the money moved through regulated rails that both parties can query. Crypto works differently. The blockchain records that a transfer happened between two addresses, but it does not record who owned them, what the transfer was for, or what the asset was worth in Canadian dollars at the time.

That gap creates three practical problems. Exchanges may ask about the source or destination of funds. Casinos may need transaction identifiers to trace a missing deposit. And because the Canada Revenue Agency treats cryptocurrency as a commodity rather than as money, moving crypto around can have implications that have nothing to do with gambling at all.

The tax question, carefully

Two separate things are often confused here, and it is worth separating them clearly.

The first is gambling winnings. In Canada, winnings from recreational gambling are generally not treated as taxable income — a longstanding position we cover in more depth in our guide to online casino play in Canada. The exception, broadly, is where gambling amounts to a business rather than a pastime, which is a fact-specific determination.

The second is the cryptocurrency itself. The CRA treats crypto as a commodity, which means disposing of it can trigger a capital gain or loss regardless of what you did with the proceeds. Converting Bitcoin to Canadian dollars is a disposition. Swapping one coin for another is generally a disposition. Whether a transfer into a casino balance counts depends on the specifics of the arrangement, and this is precisely the sort of question where the answer varies with the details.

We are not tax advisors and this is not tax advice. What we can say confidently is that the records you would need to answer these questions properly are trivial to keep at the time and painful to reconstruct later. If your crypto activity is anything beyond occasional and small, a conversation with a Canadian accountant who understands digital assets is money well spent.

What to actually record

You do not need accounting software. A spreadsheet with a row per transaction covers almost everything. For each movement of crypto in or out, capture:

  • Date and time of the transaction, including your time zone.
  • Asset and amount — the exact quantity, not a rounded figure.
  • Canadian dollar value at the time of the transaction, and where you sourced that rate.
  • Transaction hash or ID, which is the single most useful field when a deposit goes missing.
  • From and to — which exchange, wallet or casino, described plainly.
  • Network fee paid, which matters both for reconciliation and for judging whether you picked the right network.
  • Purpose in a few words: deposit, withdrawal, swap, transfer between your own wallets.

Add a screenshot folder for casino-side confirmations. When you request a withdrawal, screenshot the confirmation page showing the amount, address and timestamp. This has resolved more support disputes than any other single habit.

The source-of-funds question

Canadian players are sometimes surprised when an exchange asks about funds arriving from a gambling site, or when a casino asks about funds arriving from an unfamiliar wallet. Neither is an accusation. Both are routine compliance under anti-money-laundering obligations, and both are resolved quickly if you can produce a clear chain: this crypto was bought here on this date, moved to this wallet, deposited to this casino, and these winnings came back.

Where players get stuck is when funds have bounced through several wallets, been swapped between assets, and passed through a mixer or a privacy-focused service. Even entirely innocent activity becomes hard to explain in those conditions. Our guide to crypto gambling in Canada covers the practical trade-offs between privacy and friction in more detail.

Keeping it simple in practice

The habit that works is recording at the moment of the transaction rather than at the end of the month. When you send a deposit, copy the transaction hash into your sheet before you close the tab. It takes seconds while the information is in front of you and is genuinely tedious to recover afterwards.

A few other practices worth adopting:

Use a dedicated wallet for gambling activity rather than mixing it with long-term holdings. This makes the chain of funds obvious to anyone who asks and keeps your records clean. Export your exchange transaction history at least once a year — exchanges close, restrict Canadian users, or lose historical data, and an export you already hold is worth more than one you assume you can request later. Record the Canadian dollar value at the time of each transaction rather than planning to look up historical rates, because reconstructing rates across dozens of transactions is where most of the work ends up.

Finally, keep the casino side of the record too. Most crypto casinos provide a transaction history in your account, but access to it ends the moment an account is closed or an operator exits the Canadian market. If your play is meaningful in size, export it periodically.

The bottom line

Crypto casinos offer real advantages for Canadian players — fast settlement, low fees on the right networks, and fewer declined payments than card deposits. What they do not offer is the automatic paper trail that comes free with a bank transfer. Filling that gap yourself costs a couple of minutes per session and removes almost every scenario in which a missing deposit or a compliance question becomes a serious problem.
